news.title: Fighting to Fail
news.text:
Nuclear weapons introduced a new concept in war: no longer using our arsenal in order to win.

There was an interesting episode towards the end of World War II. The Japanese built three massive submarines with actual hangar decks for three planes each. The losing Japanese leadership sent them toward Los Angeles and had the nine planes painted in U.S. markings. The plan was to fly them from the Pacific to the City of Angels and drop the bubonic plague and other pathogens on the populace. At the last minute, Japanese leadership determined that the American response to such an act would be so extreme that they instructed their crews to dump the planes in the ocean and return home. The U.S. got one of the boats after the war for analysis. Needless to say, the U.S. never went for the underwater aircraft carrier concept beyond cruise missiles.

Until the advent of nuclear weapons, countries fought with the best they had: weapons, men, strategy, topography. The first time when punches were pulled would seem to be poison gases. They were used heavily in World War I, and both sides suffered horrific outcomes as a result. There was a formal agreement against their use, but their absence would seem more to be based on a simple understanding: any side that used such weapons could expect to receive them right back. Other than chemical weapons, everything was thrown from one side to the other: machine guns, planes, tanks, mines, artillery. Nobody thought about keeping war-fighting material back when there was a need. The U.S. invented proximity fuses and used them solely in the Pacific so that they would not fall into enemy hands. They significantly reduced the number of rounds needed to knock out Japanese planes attacking U.S. naval vessels. When things were looking bad during the Battle of the Bulge, the U.S. relented and brought the advanced fuses to the European theater.

Then came the bomb. Its destructive power was enormous. The crews that dropped the atomic weapons on Japan felt the shock waves as their planes made desperate moves to get quickly away from the detonation point. People were vaporized, as were entire structures. Those not killed outright often suffered terrible injuries that were documented by U.S. forces, scientists, and doctors who had access to Hiroshima and Nagasaki around a month after the bombings occurred. One cannot overstate the gruesome effects of what, by today’s standards, would be pretty crude bombs. I saw a new B61 bomb that was compact and aerodynamic. It has 35 times the destructive power of the bombs dropped on Japan.

With the creation of such horrific weapons, a new military strategy developed that led to failures in Korea, Vietnam, and beyond: since the atomic bombs were so destructive, we would not, never, not a chance ever again use our full arsenal for victory. No, those bombs were meant for a second strike after the U.S. was a smoldering piece of rubble. The thinking went beyond just nuclear bombs. Now we couldn’t attack terrorists when they were in civilian centers. We couldn’t use our heaviest and most deadly conventional bombs in civilian areas where the bad guys hunkered down. Israel has again failed to kill a top terrorist because it chose too small a bomb to get the job done. The bad guys ain’t dumb: they started to hide in mosques, schools, and hospitals. The sheer horror of October 7 meant that Israel slightly overcame this mental disability and attacked where the terrorists were, including a recent bombing of Nasser Hospital in Gaza, where a top Hamas commander was supposedly seriously injured.

You might conclude by now that I am somehow a nephew of Dr. Strangelove. No, I am not suggesting using nuclear weapons on Iran or any U.S. enemies. What I am suggesting is that the current “rules of engagement” and “laws of warfare” always work against the good guys, whom I will choose as the U.S., Western Europe, and Israel. The bad guys, including Iran and all of its satellites as well as America’s more traditional enemies, know these self-imposed limitations and exploit them to the maximum. War is violent, and civilians have died in every conflict since the first one was fought. There is an enormous difference between firing an RPG at a civilian car, as Hamas did in southern Israel, versus firing a Merkava tank round at a building housing terrorists, killing them and the family living above them. The press, the U.N., the nudniks from The Hague, the lefties, and, of course, Muslims themselves love to invoke some imaginary rules of engagement that somehow only apply to one side. Israel is accused of genocide when it is the first country in history to feed its enemy during active combat and send SMS and drone-based messages telling the locals to move. I wish Israel would stop this nonsense. Identify, bomb, destroy, and repeat. The war would have been over in six months if it had been fought for victory and not Hague-style points. The U.S. could have finished off Iran in a few weeks if it had fired everything south of a nuclear bomb. Instead, many targets were spared, and the war is not over.

One thing to note is that our enemies have no such compunction about keeping certain weapons off the field of play. There is talk of Iran trying to use a “dirty” radiological bomb in Washington. There is that old saying that if Israel dropped its weapons, the Palestinians would kill every Jew; if the Palestinians dropped their weapons, there would be peace. There is no weapon held by Hamas or Iran that they would not use against infidels. Only the West, from the days of Harry Truman, pulls its punches and ends up with ties or losses. Truman suggested that he might drop a thermonuclear bomb. He didn’t, and the peninsula is still divided, with the North having nuclear bombs of its own.

Marco Rubio and Donald Trump have done well to publicly chide the International Criminal Court at The Hague. The Nuremberg Trials seemed like a good idea when the good guys won, and their people were the judges. Now, lefty losers and ideologues stand in judgment of Israel fighting off a psychotic terrorist group that burned children alive and killed families whole. The rules can only apply to Israel and the Western countries, and that has to end. I am not asking that Western armies become as depraved as their enemies. All I ask is that they identify legitimate targets and destroy them. Nobody in the Eighth Air Force asked about civilians living around the ball-bearing factory in Schweinfurt. If the factory could be destroyed, German tanks and planes could not be made. The West has to realize that war is hell and the more violent it is, the faster it is over. Why did World War II take four years to victory while 20 years in Afghanistan led to the Taliban having the best American-equipped army in the region?

If nuclear weapons are truly required to finish off Pickaxe Mountain, then use them. If Iran’s electricity production needs to go to zero for the mullahs to be driven from power, then turn off the lights. Start with your goal — as the Allies did (“unconditional surrender”) — and then work backward for every step to reach it. Stopping and starting war and attacking peripheral targets do not work. Fight to win and then go home victorious. There is no substitute for victory. Not the number of weapons delivered, the number of sorties, the accuracy of weapons delivered... no, just victory.

Use everything you’ve got and stop apologizing. They would use those weapons if they had them. Don’t give them the chance to get them.

news.title: Iran War: Among Democrats, Is Fetterman the Only Sign of Intelligent Life?
news.text:
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., stands virtually alone as a congressional Democrat who worries about a nuclear-armed Iran, or more precisely, who worries that the possibility of a nuclear-armed Iran should be dealt with and dealt with now.

Our allies, including those in Europe and Canada, appear to think similarly about Iran. They are far more consumed by their hatred of President Donald Trump than by worrying about a fanatical regime that vows to destroy them if allowed the opportunity. Their eyes remain shut even after the American-Israeli war has demonstrated that Iran possesses missile capabilities to reach targets far beyond what the intelligence analysts thought possible.

Our allies remain unperturbed even as the war has again shown the Iranian leadership's willingness to do anything to retain power, including but not limited to killing an estimated 40,000 unarmed Iranians, placing civilians in front of military targets and cutting off 20 percent of the world's oil supply to fight its enemies.

In July, Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., appeared in an episode of comedian Theo Von's podcast "This Past Weekend" and discussed why Trump acted and why he did so now:

"Our intelligence, here's what our intelligence showed, and I've seen it. It's classified, but I've seen it. But I can give you a general outline.

"Our intelligence showed that Iran was building up its missile capacity, both ballistic and cruise, and they were going to compile so many missiles and drones that they were going to turn to America and Israel and say, 'We're restarting our nuclear weapons program. And if you try to stop us, we're going to destroy the rest of the Middle East. And by the way, our missiles can now reach London and Paris, Paris and Germany.'

"And President Trump was faced with, well, 'Do I let them continue?' He had already bombed their nuclear — some of their nuclear facilities. But he was faced with the decision, 'Do I let them get to the point where they have so many missiles and drones, ballistic and cruise, that they could destroy the Middle East, that they could hit London, that they might even be able to hit the United States? Or do I go in to stop them?' And he did. ...

"We cannot let these people have a nuclear weapon. These people are stone-cold crazy."

One might have thought that Kennedy's public revelation might have caused our allies finally to sit up straight and pay just a bit more attention to the peril of Iran, if not actually join the fight.

But as to Europe, its collective welfare-state economies run at half-speed compared to the U.S. economy. Young Europeans, restless and angry about their future precisely because of their suffocating welfare state and decades of legal and illegal immigration, could not care less about what future they would have if Iran had nuclear weapons.

Under pressure from Trump, our NATO allies, except for Spain, agreed to spend 5 percent of their GDP on defense when most were not spending the previous benchmark of 2 percent. With the street protests in countries like France over alleged underinvestment in public education, it's difficult to see how the new NATO commitment can possibly be met.

Stateside, the incoming congressional Democrats not only oppose the Iran war, save Fetterman, but publicly promise to cut off funding to stop it. They correctly blame Trump's decision to go to war on rising gas prices, but apparently believe Trump woke up eight months ago and decided to bomb Iran rather than to play a round of golf.

The No. 1 concern of midterm voters is the economy, with the majority saying they are economically worse off since Trump 2.0. Gas prices before the war dropped to a five-year low, with some places in the country with gas under $2 a gallon. When the war ends, lower gas prices will return. In fact, prices month to month have already dropped.

The "affordability" demands of the Democrats and democratic socialists lead right to the protests we witness today in the streets of London, Paris and Rome. The brass ring is Medicare for All, a government healthcare takeover that 75 percent of its advocates falsely believe can be paid for by taxing the aforementioned billions who, of course, do not pay their fair share.

Someone once said, "You have a thousand problems -- until you lose your health. Then you have one problem." The world will have one problem if it ignores Iran's determination to get a nuclear bomb.

Just ask Fetterman.

news.title: We Can’t Tolerate Any More Republican Incompetence
news.text:
With all the postmortems on why we screwed up so badly in the midterm elections, it’s pretty clear that one thing we have to be able to do as Republicans is actually govern. I’m talking competence. I’m talking about being capable of performing basic tasks like keeping order, filling potholes, and teaching kids to read. That’s something Democrats can’t do, but even if they could, they won’t want to. Competence doesn’t factor into the Democrats' equation. They’re solely about power. The best thing about being conservative, as far as governance goes, is that we want to do as little as possible and therefore be as efficient as possible. But why aren’t we making this obvious play? Why aren’t we owning the competence issue?

Things keep getting screwed up, and it keeps screwing up the Republicans. If you’re going to have a government that tells you you can’t have endless stuff for free, the implied obligation of such daddy government is to provide a government that performs the basics well. But just the other day, as hundreds of us were getting ready to join the Salem/Townhall Gulf of America cruise — ahoy, I’m writing this from Jamaica — the entire civilian aviation system collapsed. It just stopped. And why? No one seems really sure, which itself isn’t something that’s particularly great. The Republicans are in charge, and this sort of thing isn’t supposed to happen. We’re supposed to make the trains run on time, as opposed to Democrats, who can’t even build a mile of track for $100 billion.

Populism has its attractions. It is one way to ensure the ruling class considers the needs and desires of regular people and integrates them into government operations. For example, illegal aliens — we were told for years we couldn’t even complain about them. Now we’re deporting them left and right, as you can hear from the screaming of the whiners who think that every third-world refugee should get a car, a cell phone, and free dental care in the USA on our dime.

But populism, for all its positive aspects, doesn’t deal with the nitty-gritty of governing. It’s not interested in the nitty-gritty of governing. In fact, populists seem to treat it as a dodge or a scam when someone objects that a populist wish can’t come true with a wave of the wand. Let’s look at the SAVE Act. It’s a populist icon. We would all love the SAVE Act to pass. But there are procedural reasons why that’s not going to happen, having to do with the filibuster and the fact that a bunch of Republicans won’t come aboard. As a practical matter, the SAVE Act would be tremendously hard, though not impossible, to pass within the context of the existing system. If you want to get rid of the system, which is a populist move, that’s a whole different thing. It’s also a much harder thing.

Now, I’m not covering for John Thune. It’s John Thune’s job to get it done, and that’s a binary choice. You either get it done despite it being hard, or you don’t get to have the job. Well, except now, the Republicans have given him the job again. The guy didn’t get it done, and they’ve given him the job. If you can’t get the job done, you’re not supposed to keep the job. Why are we rewarding failure? And again, I understand it’s really hard to do this. But I don’t care. I want it done. And it didn’t get done. Yes, I know there are reasons for that. Again, I don’t care.

As my drill sergeant once said, excuses are like a certain body part, and everyone’s got one, and they all stink. We need to be the Get It Done Party. We need to be the Make It Happen Party. But some of us have unrealistic expectations, and some of us have no expectations at all. It’s easy to be a Republican and fall into the Democrat trap of ignoring results. We had generations of Republicans like that, and while we got rid of a few of them during this midterm election — you can’t paint anything all black — we still have a number of them who are perfectly happy to walk into the Capitol, punch the figurative clock, and collect their pay, prestige, and power. What’s funny is how offended they get when we expect them to accomplish something.

But we need to get back to expecting Republicans to accomplish something, because that’s one key way we’ll differentiate ourselves from Democrats among the winnable suburban voters who used to vote for us. Now, the urban voters are gone. All they care about is the scraps they get tossed to them from the table. They’ve had well over half a century to vote as if they cared about their children’s education, or the crime in their streets, or anything except making sure their EBT and Section 8 were maxed out. They are pure clients, caring about nothing except the next subsidy and willing to live in the festering Petri dish of social pathologies that they’ve made.

But the suburbanite former Republicans, the kind of guys who wear Dockers and women who drive minivans and who are currently voting for Democrats, in significant part because the men can’t be Trump and Trump doesn’t want the women, look at things differently. They don’t really expect to get things directly from the government. They expect government to do things correctly. They don’t want criminals on their streets. That’s why in neighborhoods like mine, full of blue voters, a stranger walking down the street is going to get rousted by three cop cars, and all the Chardonnay wine women with the “Hate Has No Home” signs in front of their condos are going to applaud.

Democrats won’t do things because Democrats can’t do things and don’t care to do things. They’re about redistribution, not execution. We need to be about execution, sometimes literally. Republicans need to reestablish themselves as the ones who keep criminals off the streets. They need to reestablish themselves as the ones who make sure that schools function. They need to reestablish themselves as the ones who get the potholes filled.

Now, they’re going to get opposition to this stuff, but that’s not necessarily bad. When Democrats start siding with criminals publicly, we tend to win. We’ve seen this since the ’60s — when Democrats start coddling criminals, normal people start voting Republican again. And when they stop, as Bill Clinton did in 1992, voters tend to give Democrats a shot. The schools and pothole stuff is a little more difficult because you’re dealing with government employees. Nobody cries like a government employee at the cruel injustice that is demanding that they perform their jobs, so that has to be handled deftly so as not to scandalize the soft and spineless. But it can happen. Republicans tend to win when people trust them to make government function correctly.

But lately, with things like the airline disaster, it looks like nobody here knows how to play this damn game. As much as I support the Iran War — I’m all for annihilating generational enemies who’ve maimed and murdered thousands of Americans — we haven’t got it done. It’s not that we can’t. It’s that we’ve chosen a path that means we can’t play to our strength, which is getting things done.

We’ve got to get back to that. We’ve got to get back to making things happen. You need to be the party of competence. It works. Glenn Youngkin won in blue Virginia as a competence guy. His successor didn’t give off competence vibes, and she lost. Greg Abbott had 12 years to impress his voters with his competence. They felt things weren’t going in the right direction, and they fired him in favor of a communist half-wit who will, soon enough, make the Lone Star State yearn for its erstwhile governor.

Executive competence. That’s the key. And for the Republicans, that’s going to be an edge for guys like Ron DeSantis, who has proven his competence. The same with Marco Rubio, who oversees the State Department. Hopefully, Donald Trump will give JD Vance the authority to do things to show his competence — the fraud portfolio is a vital one and a huge opportunity for him. But regardless, whoever comes next is only going to win if people get sick of Democrats who talk a good game and get nothing done and turn to the Republicans to make things happen.

Not being competent is political incompetence.

news.title: Ted Cruz Says Democrats Are in 'Civil War' After Cornyn Clash
news.text: Texas U.S. Senator Ted Cruz is claiming Democrats are in a "civil war" over the party's future, even as reports emerged of a heated confrontation between the Texas Republican and fellow Senator John Cornyn on the Senate floor. "Democrats are in a CIVIL WAR right now," Cruz wrote on X while promoting the latest episode of his Verdict podcast. "What's clear: The radicals are saying the Democrats weren't radical enough. They want more crazy!" In the episode, Cruz pointed to leadership battles among Senate Democrats as evidence of growing divisions within the party. Since their overwhelming midterm victory, an internal fight has erupted over whether Chuck Schumer should lead the incoming Senate majority or step aside in favor of challenger Chris Van Hollen. "One of the really unfortunate consequences of the election is the Democrats in Congress have gotten much more radical," Cruz said on the podcast. "They have moved left dramatically." He argued that a challenge to Senate Democratic leadership reflected pressure from the party's progressive wing and claimed, "The radicals are saying the Democrats weren't radical enough. They want more crazy." Clash With Cornyn Cruz's comments came after reports of a rare public dispute between Texas' two Republican senators. According to multiple reporters present in the Senate, Cornyn confronted Cruz on the Senate floor Tuesday following a dispute over the nomination of T. Elliot Gaiser, an Ohio lawyer, to a federal judgeship for the Northern District of Texas. Cornyn told the Washington Sun he wasn't sure why Cruz would nominate someone who wasn't a Texas lawyer. "I don't find you credible. I'm mad at you!" Cornyn reportedly shouted at Cruz, according to multiple accounts. Reporters also said Cornyn could be heard swearing during the confrontation and shouting that someone had "ended my career," though accounts differed on whether he was referring to Cruz, President Donald Trump or another figure involved in the dispute. Neither senator immediately commented publicly on the exchange. Newsweek reached out to the offices of Cruz and Cornyn for comment. Why Tensions Have Been Building The clash follows years of friction between the two Texas Republicans, tensions that have intensified amid battles over federal judicial nominations and Cornyn's political standing within the GOP. Cornyn was defeated in the Republican primary for his reelection bid by beleaguered Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was then defeated handily by Democrat James Talarico. The immediate dispute reportedly centered on a judicial nomination for a federal judgeship in Dallas that Cornyn moved to block. The confrontation came as the Trump administration and its allies have increasingly scrutinized senators viewed as insufficiently supportive of the president's judicial and political agenda. Cornyn has also faced mounting pressure from the party's pro-Trump wing in recent years. The senator lost his bid for Senate Republican leader in 2024 and has repeatedly drawn criticism from Trump-aligned activists over issues including gun legislation, Ukraine funding and Senate leadership fights. Cruz, meanwhile, has aligned himself more closely with Trump's political movement and has used his podcast and public appearances to criticize what he describes as establishment Republicans. Democrats in Cruz's Sights On his podcast, however, Cruz focused his attention on Democrats, portraying internal leadership contests as a struggle between party leaders and a more progressive faction. "The Marxists and the Islamists are empowered," Cruz said during the discussion. He also argued that even if Senate Democratic leaders survive challenges from the left, the contests themselves would push the party further in a progressive direction. "Whether this leadership challenge succeeds or not, it is going to move Schumer and the entire conference to the left," Cruz said. news.title: Trump opposes robust AI regulation, says it would stifle super intelligence development
news.text:
President Donald Trump warned that any “robust” regulation of artificial intelligence, or super intelligence as he terms it, would “stifle” development — even as the US imposes new restrictions on access to advanced AI technology.

In remarks to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, Trump said AI is “almost completely good, but it’s got some bad elements, and we have to be very careful in managing those bad elements.” 

But “we oppose any form of robust regulation or anything to control and stifle SI, and we won’t allow that to happen, frankly,” he told foreign leaders in the plenary session, using his preferred term for super intelligence.

His remarks come days after the US moved to limit several countries from providing Chinese companies with remote access to advanced AI chips and servers. They also come as fallout from the alleged espionage scandal that’s embroiled Nvidia Corp. and its former CEO Jensen Huang has overshadowed Trump’s trip to Asia for a pair of international summits.

Huang, who played an outsized role in shaping the White House approach to China and AI policy more generally, admitted to an affair with a woman now under investigation by the US government for potentially working with a Chinese spy agency and possibly helping smuggle chips.

Hawks Emboldened

Though Trump has defended the former CEO, the episode has emboldened China hawks in Congress, who are renewing a push for stricter export controls.

Amid the blowback, the Commerce Department issued a rule that would require data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil to obtain a US government license before exporting advanced AI chips from Nvidia and other American manufacturers to customers in those countries. The measure seeks to restrict China and other US adversaries from accessing offshore computing power that uses American-designed processors.

Trump is due to meet with Xi on the sidelines of APEC later on Thursday, but has played down the Nvidia scandal as a topic he plans to discuss with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping.

news.title: Trump Defends Jensen Huang in China: ‘Take Care of Our Geniuses’
news.text: President Donald Trump traveled to Shenzhen, China's high-tech capital, to sit down with Chinese President Xi Jinping. But in a television interview there, he spent several minutes defending Jensen Huang, the former Nvidia chief executive whose fall has unsettled Washington and Wall Street alike. "We have to take care of our geniuses; by the way, we don't have that many of them," Trump told Fox News Senior White House Correspondent Jacqui Heinrich in an interview that aired Wednesday on The Ingraham Angle. "When we have brilliant people like Jensen, we can't say, oh, you know, he did this or that. We have to take care." The remarks came less than one week after Jensen Huang resigned as president, chief executive officer and a director of Nvidia, the company he co-founded in 1993 and built into one of the most valuable corporations in the world. His exit followed reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a businesswoman some U.S. intelligence officials suspected of gathering information for Beijing — though there is no public evidence he knowingly assisted Chinese intelligence. And it came a day after Nvidia's board said, flatly, that it would not bring him back. Jensen Huang now faces Congress. He has agreed to closed-door, transcribed interviews with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China Select committees on December 1. Senator Tim Scott, the South Carolina Republican who chairs the Senate Banking Committee, said Wednesday that Jensen Huang has also agreed to appear before that panel, though no date has been set. 'Some People Can't Be Replaced' Trump cast the episode not as a breach but as a loss. "It's a tragedy. He's such a brilliant man," he said. Of Nvidia's directors, he added: "The board sounds like, you know, they have their own ideas, but you can't replace people. Some people can't be replaced." The president made his case in the vocabulary of engineering. Nvidia's Blackwell processor, he said, was "10 years ahead" of any competitor and so intricate that "it can't be copied" — unlike Hollywood films that, in his telling, are pirated and "all over the world" within two hours of release. Then he reached for a precedent closer to home. "I helped Elon a lot in my first term. I helped him a lot. He was in big trouble," Trump said of Elon Musk. "And now we have a guy that's sending up rockets and landing them." Without that help, he said, "You wouldn't probably have Elon today. We have to take care of our geniuses. There aren't that many of them." Heinrich then asked whether the affair amounted to a national security concern. "I haven't heard that she was a spy," Trump said, according to Fox News' account of the exchange. "She was a business woman who bought chips." A Founder's Swift Fall The crisis began October 29, when The New York Times reported U.S. intelligence links between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that is among Nvidia's largest customers in Southeast Asia. The two are not related. CNN sources have since said the intelligence does not prove Alice Huang was spying, with officials divided over the strength of the evidence. China denies trying to ensnare Jensen Huang, and Megaspeed has said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny." On November 8, Jensen Huang wrote to employees acknowledging that he had been unfaithful to his wife. "Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life," he wrote. "I have fallen short of that responsibility." The board opened an independent investigation that day and expressed confidence in him. Within days, the Times reported a second relationship, with an executive who reported directly to Jensen Huang, and Reuters reported a third. A regulatory filing shows the board accepted the resignation on November 11; the company made it public the following morning and named Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive officer. Nvidia shares fell 14 percent at the opening bell before paring most of those losses. A Door Closed in Public On Tuesday, Jensen Huang wrote on X, "I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," and said he "would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO" if the board judged it in the company's interest. Hours later, on Nvidia's quarterly earnings call, Board Chair Harvey Jones gave his answer: "The NVIDIA board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." The same call reported record quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion. The President's Steady Defense Trump has stood by Jensen Huang throughout. On November 9, before the resignation, he told reporters that Jensen Huang had said he "had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy." On November 12, he wrote on Truth Social that Jensen Huang "has done a fantastic job" and urged Nvidia to hire former Apple Chief Executive Officer Tim Cook: "A Legend replaces a Legend!" On November 16, as he left the White House for Asia, he told reporters he "would not mind" seeing Jensen Huang reinstated, adding, "I think he learned a big lesson." Musk has made the same case. “There’s no one that can really replace Jensen,” he said Wednesday at The New York Times DealBook Summit, likening Jensen Huang’s ouster to the Chicago Bulls kicking Michael Jordan off the team during a winning streak. Congress Is Still Asking Questions On Capitol Hill, Jensen Huang's resignation has not ended the questions. "Jensen Huang's decision to resign from NVIDIA does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, wrote on X. "They still owe Congress answers." Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat, wrote that Congress "must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia" and asked what the Trump administration did once it learned of the relationship. The pressure is bipartisan. Representative John Moolenaar, the Michigan Republican who chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said in a statement that the departure was a "firing" and "an unfortunate end that could have been avoided," but warned that "American companies should never jeopardize our nation's security by giving Chinese companies access to their most advanced chips." When Jensen Huang sits down with House investigators on December 1, the argument Trump made in Shenzhen — that genius earns a measure of protection — will meet lawmakers who say it buys no exemption from answers.
news.summary: Trump defends ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid a China spy scandal, saying America must ‘take care of our geniuses.’
news.author: Lars Hanson

news.title: ‘It Was a Mistake for Trump to Meet Putin One-on-One Without Ukraine,’ Zelensky Tells NBC
news.text:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said it was a mistake for US President Donald Trump to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin one-on-one without Ukraine’s participation, arguing that Washington and Beijing could force Moscow to end its war if they were willing to use their economic leverage.

In an exclusive interview with NBC News correspondent Richard Engel in Kyiv, Zelensky said Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping had enough power to stop Putin through coordinated sanctions and restrictions on trade with Russia.

The remarks came ahead of Thursday’s Nov. 19 summit in Shenzhen, China, where Trump, Putin and Xi were scheduled to discuss Russia’s war without Ukrainian or European representatives present.

Zelensky argued that the US and China could force Moscow toward a ceasefire by imposing sanctions or even threatening to do so.

If Washington and Beijing took such action against Russia, “that’s the end of the war,” Zelensky said.

He maintained that Trump and Xi had “enough power to stop Putin” in a single meeting.

Asked whether their failure to exert that pressure would indicate a lack of political will, Zelensky replied: “That is exactly what it means.”

Zelensky Dismisses Putin’s War Justification as Nonsense

Zelensky also dismissed the Kremlin’s longstanding justification for invading Ukraine – the claim that Russia was protecting Russian-speaking Ukrainians from alleged persecution.

Nearly five years into the full-scale invasion, Russian forces continue to bombard Ukrainian cities, including predominantly Russian-speaking communities, undermining Moscow’s claim that its war was launched to protect them.

“They always claimed they came to Ukraine to protect Russian-speaking people,” Zelensky said.

The Kremlin has repeatedly invoked the supposed persecution of Russian speakers and allegations of Ukrainian “Nazism” to justify its invasion, claims Kyiv has rejected as fabricated pretexts for territorial conquest.

Zelensky Asked About Russian Assassination Threats

Zelensky also addressed threats against his own life, acknowledging that Russian assassination plots remained a danger but insisting that fear could not dictate how he governed Ukraine.

In a personal exchange, Engel asked whether Zelensky feared Putin might target him directly, particularly as Ukrainian forces intensified long-range strikes inside Russia.

Engel referred to reports that Putin had lifted a ban on targeting Zelensky personally, although those reports were not independently confirmed.

Zelensky did not dismiss the possibility.

“We all want to live,” he said. “And of course every normal person wants to live and doesn’t want to die.”

But Ukrainians, he explained, were fighting with the knowledge that defending their country could cost them their lives.

“We live and fight understanding that we can die defending our country and the future of our children and grandchildren,” Zelensky said.

Engel pressed him directly: Would he be willing to die for Ukraine?

Zelensky responded by emphasizing his responsibilities rather than his personal sacrifice.

“We do our job and we fight and do what we have to do,” he said.

“I’m a president, I do what I have to do.”

The Ukrainian leader said Russian operatives had previously prepared several assassination attempts against him.

He expressed doubt that future plots would succeed but acknowledged receiving repeated warnings from intelligence services, bodyguards and media reports.

Security officials sometimes urged him to change his movements, schedule and daily routine to reduce the danger.

But Zelensky said he could not spend every day thinking about whether Russia might succeed in killing him.

“I can’t focus on it,” he said.

For Zelensky, allowing such threats to control his life would contradict the very purpose of Ukraine’s resistance.

“We fight for freedom,” he said.
news.summary: In an NBC interview, Zelensky criticizes Trump’s one-on-one talks with Putin without Kyiv, urges US-China economic pressure on Moscow, dismisses Russia’s war justification and addresses threats against his life.

Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit to defend American interests, confront Beijing and Moscow over security concerns and avoid making concessions that could undermine Ukraine and US news.title: Deutsche Bank leak: How 15m files put the bank on the spot
news.text: Dubai: A German data protection authority has launched an investigation into Deutsche Bank after a leak of 15 million internal records surfaced, a Reuters report showed.Alexander Rossnagel, the data protection commissioner for Hesse, announced the probe on Wednesday, November 18. His office will examine whether the bank had adequate data protection measures in place. It will also check whether the lender reported the leak on time. “I am investigating whether Deutsche Bank promptly notified the affected individuals,” Rossnagel said. He has requested further information and documents from the bank.Deutsche Bank told Reuters it proactively informed the appropriate authorities about the leak..How the leak surfacedThe records emerged on November 17 under the banner “Inside Deutsche Bank”. Barracuda Media, a South African nonprofit, coordinated the project. More than 200 journalists have worked on the files since spring, and dozens of outlets published findings simultaneously. Journalists Josy Joseph and Khadija Sharife obtained the material from two whistleblowers.The trove includes more than nine million emails, plus presentations, board minutes, compliance files and chat logs. The documents reach back to the early 2010s. Reuters notes it could not immediately verify the reports..What the files revealEpstein: Deutsche Bank flagged payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein worth $582 million in 2019 suspicious activity reports. Senate investigators had earlier uncovered about $250 million.Trump: On March 30, 2017, a relationship manager sent year-end tax statements for 1,586 private accounts to one client’s accountant. Donald Trump’s account was among them. The accountant alerted the bank and deleted the file. The bank informed the Federal Reserve Bank of New York but not the affected clients, according to the reporting.Trump rejected the bank’s conduct during a trip to Manila. “They shouldn’t have done it. It’s illegal for them to do it,” he said. Deutsche Bank declined to comment on his reaction.Russia: The documents show the bank planned to expand in Russia shortly before the invasion of Ukraine. Internal compliance staff raised warnings. Chief Executive Christian Sewing sat on the working group that developed the strategy, the files indicate. The Russian unit employed 162 people and earned €61 million ($67 million) before tax in the prior year. The files also detail tax-planning models built for wealthy clients..The bank’s responseDeutsche Bank says the matters “date back many years, in some cases as much as two decades”. It reviewed them at the time, worked with regulators and has since strengthened controls. The bank calls itself a “different, stronger and safer bank” today. It expects no significant financial impact.However, the German government has demanded transparency and said that an independent regulators and law enforcement must examine the material. A member of the European Parliament has urged Sewing to appear before the legislature..Shares take the hitThe stock closed at €32.915 in Frankfurt on November 16. On November 17, it fell as much as 6.4% to €30.82. That marked the steepest one-day drop since March. At the low, roughly €2.8 billion vanished from market value.New York-listed shares closed down 5.47%, or $1.96, at $33.88. Frankfurt trading on Wednesday extended the slide by another 1.9% in the early session.The sell-off follows a strong run. Deutsche Bank shares nearly doubled in 2025 on record profits, and the bank has posted strong results in recent quarters. The stock touched €34.26 in January, then tumbled to €23.82 on March 22. It recovered to a 52-week high of €35.845 before this week’s drop.Analysts see the shares as undervalued. The Street target sits near $40.50. The market’s attention now turns to the regulatory findings and any fallout for Sewing.

news.title: Trump Breaks From World Leaders for Red Carpet Moment
news.text:
President Donald Trump broke from his fellow world leaders to have a solo red carpet moment in China.

Trump, 80, was in Shenzhen on Wednesday for the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting, including Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

When Trump arrived at the site of the meeting, he walked slowly across the red carpet before pausing to pose for photographs in front of the assembled media.

The White House Press Pool X account noted he was the only world leader to pause for a solo red-carpet shot, with everyone else walking across the carpet without stopping.

“After pausing for a long moment, Trump smiled, said thank you, and continued his walk,” the Pool reported.

At one point in his show, host Anderson Cooper interrupted a segment with CNN reporter Fareed Zakaria to play the footage of Trump pausing for his red carpet moment.

“This is why he’s done it,” Zakaria said. “He wants these photographs, the symbolism, the harkening back to superpower summits of the 1980s, perhaps even Yalta.”

The Yalta Conference in 1945, the year before Trump was born, was a World War II summit to shape the postwar world, featuring U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, U.K. Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Russian leader Joseph Stalin.

“Yalta... was the three powers that won World War II, deciding on the fate of the world,” Zakaria said. “This is a photo op. This is a completely symbolic meeting. They’re not going to get any substantive agreements.”

Pointing out the absence of Ukraine and the European Union from the summit, Zakaria said, “It makes no strategic sense; it makes television sense.”

At that point, Cooper cut to live footage of Putin entering, noting, “He was not pausing for photographs as the president did, walking through.”

Following his solo photo, Trump also posed with the leaders for an APEC family photo.

After Trump entered the room, the Pool reports he was shown his place at the center of the group before the photo was taken.

The U.S. president shook hands with Canadian leader Mark Carney, whom he has regularly clashed with, before Xi stood between Trump and Putin for the photo.

“Trump chatted briefly with Carney before he & President Xi led the group out of the room,” the Pool noted, noting the group photo took just two minutes.

The 80-year-old’s red carpet moment follows another awkward appearance in China.

Trump took twice as long as other world leaders to walk the red carpet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation welcome banquet in Shenzhen on Wednesday.

He took over a minute to enter the venue, stopping multiple times to pose for cameras. 

The Daily Beast has contacted the White House for comment.

news.text:
US President Donald Trump has renewed his warning that he intends to end the conflict with Iran "soon", insisting that any agreement with Tehran must be durable enough to survive future changes in American leadership.

In an interview with Fox, an excerpt of which was circulated by the White House-affiliated Rapid Response 47 account (@RapidResponse47) on X, Trump said he wanted a long-term agreement rather than a temporary arrangement that could be reversed by a successor.

"I want a deal that can be lasting. If we have a bad President, a weak President, I want a deal that will supersede the President," Trump said.

He also reiterated his determination to bring the confrontation to an end.

"I'm going to finish it off — soon. One way or the other, we'll finish it off," he added.

The remarks highlight Trump's twin-track approach to Iran: keeping diplomatic channels open while maintaining military and economic pressure on Tehran.

In the wider Fox News interview, Trump confirmed that Washington remained in contact with Iranian representatives and claimed Tehran wanted an agreement. He nevertheless insisted that any settlement must prevent Iran from rebuilding its military and nuclear capabilities.

"Yeah, we talked to them. We talked to them. They want to make a deal, but I want a deal that can be lasting," he said.

Trump did not provide a proposed agreement, negotiating timetable or specific mechanism that would guarantee a future US administration could not reverse the arrangement.

news.text:
Garcia’s targets break down into three categories. First are those Trump figures who appear to have enriched themselves either by their official position or their proximity to the president. Second are those who have been involved in policy initiatives that Democrats find objectionable. And third are those whom Democrats can portray as having been involved, even tangentially, in the Jeffrey Epstein matter. (The Democrats’ homepage on the oversight committee website features a photo of Trump and Epstein in Palm Beach together 29 years ago, in 1997.)

Put succinctly, some parts of the planned oversight will be legitimate, while others will be pure politics.

The Trump family enrichment falls into the legitimate category. In the World Liberty Financial matter, there are reports the Trumps made $1.4 billion, mostly from licensing the Trump name for the sale of crypto tokens that soon lost most of their value. In separate letters to Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, Garcia wrote that “Oversight Democrats have found that your roles as a co-founder of World Liberty Financial and a key player in the Trump family’s pay-to-play schemes have raked in billions of dollars for the Trump family over the past several years.”

In a letter to Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner, the president’s envoy for both the war in Iran and the war in Ukraine, Garcia charged that “directly or indirectly, you have received billions of dollars in fees and investments with particularly troubling ties to Middle East states where you also have a government role.”

Outside of Trump’s family, Garcia also sent a letter to longtime Trump figure Corey Lewandowski, who for a while played a top role, without an official position, at the Department of Homeland Security. “Almost immediately upon entering DHS as a special government employee, allegations arose that you abused your position in the Trump administration and close relationships to President Trump and then-Secretary Kristi Noem to enrich yourself,” Garcia wrote.

Garcia’s letters show that overseers will have some reasonable questions to ask. But the second category of investigation, Trump policy initiatives, will likely fall into the category of plain old politics. The top Democratic target will be new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, who has been a dominant player in the Trump crackdown on illegal immigration. “Members of the Trump administration have described you as the ‘linchpin’ and ‘architect’ of the Trump administration’s most extreme policies, advocating for the widespread abuse of civil liberties,” Garcia wrote. “We have documented, and will continue to document, your role in orchestrating, overseeing, and defending these abuses.”

A key fact not mentioned often by Garcia and his fellow Democrats is that the foundation of the Trump immigration crackdown is U.S. immigration law. It has been on the books for decades, and many Democrats oppose its enforcement, but it is there, and the Trump administration has largely acted within it. A Stephen Miller investigation will certainly offer Democrats an opportunity to yell and pound the table, but it seems unlikely to add up to much in the end.

Finally, there is Epstein. And on that, House Democrats appear to want to target Vice President JD Vance, who was 12 years old when, in 1996, the FBI received its first reports about alleged wrongdoing by Epstein. Democrats appear ready to accuse Vance of covering up evidence in the case, and in a letter, Garcia demands that Vance “identify every meeting that administration officials held concerning Jeffrey Epstein, the Epstein files, or the Trump administration’s response to the committee’s subpoena or the Epstein Files Transparency Act. For each meeting, include the date, location, and attendees.”

The letter asked for much, much more information. Garcia demanded that Vance produce it “no later than December 2, 2026.” The vice president might note that Democrats will not take control of the committee until Jan. 3, 2027, so he might not be in a rush to respond. Garcia sent a similar letter to former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, and another Epstein-focused letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche.

Democrats will talk a lot about “justice” in the Epstein case. But the investigation will constantly bump into the fact that the main perpetrator, Epstein, died in jail; his sidekick, Ghislaine Maxwell, is serving a 20-year prison sentence; and we already know most of what happened in the case. Garcia and his colleagues will then allege a cover-up — that’s how they hope to keep 2028 hopeful Vance connected to the investigation — but it’s unclear whether they will find anything that will change the public’s yearslong understanding of the case.

Finally, it doesn’t take a particularly sharp eye to notice that there is one recipient missing in Garcia’s list of letters: President Donald Trump himself. But it will soon be clear that the president is the main target of every single day of Garcia’s exercise in oversight.

news.title: India will not sign trade deal till new US tariff framework takes shape: Commerce secretary
news.text:
India and the United States are close to finalising negotiations for a bilateral trade agreement, but the deal will not be signed until Washington sets up a new tariffs framework, the Deccan Herald quoted Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal as saying on Wednesday.

After an interim trade deal was agreed upon on February 2, US tariffs on Indian goods would have been reduced to 18% from a combined rate of 50%. The earlier rate of 50% had included a punitive levy of 25% imposed in August 2025 over India’s purchase of Russian oil.

However, negotiations on the final deal were hampered after the US Supreme Court on February 20 struck down global tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump, ruling that he had exceeded his authority.

In response, Trump imposed a temporary 10% tariff on goods imported into the US, citing his authority under the 1974 Trade Act. This had left the status of US’ trade deals with all countries, including India, unclear.

The commerce secretary was quoted as saying that all aspects of the deal were “more or less finalised” and an interim agreement was imminent.

However, Agrawal said that the deal could only be signed after the US’ new tariff framework comes into effect and investigations under Section 301 are concluded, Moneycontrol reported. The provision allows the US to investigate and impose tariffs or trade sanctions against countries over unfair trade practices.

“You can’t have a deal till you have got uncertainty around multiple investigations or which are already there,” the commerce secretary was quoted as saying. “So, I think those numbers and the actual deal will be signed and operationalised once these investigations are over and they are [reaching maturity].”

Agrawal made the comments at an event organised by the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry.

Agrawal also said that the government was trying to conclude negotiations on some other trade deals by the end of the year with some “good news” expected in December, The Times of India reported, adding that it was seen as a reference to ongoing talks with Canada.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to visit Canada in December.

news.title: What do Trump, Putin and Xi want from their Shenzhen meeting?  - Trinidad Tribune – Latest Trinidad And
news.text:
US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold a three-way meeting on Thursday in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, the first ever between the leaders of the world’s three most powerful militaries.

The meeting, which will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, has drawn comparisons with the 1945 wartime Yalta conference at which the United States, United Kingdom and then-Soviet Union agreed on the post-war order. But those powers had been allied during a world war. Analysts say the three men meeting on Thursday are arriving with very different goals, and that few concrete outcomes can be expected.

“It’s a summit of Trump’s ego, Putin’s tactics, China’s strategy,” Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera.

So what does each leader want from this meeting?

What is this meeting about?

The trilateral meeting is taking place on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ summit, which China is hosting in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. Trump travelled to China after attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meeting in Manila.

The White House has said that Trump plans to discuss the war with Iran as well as a possible three-way agreement on nuclear armament with Xi and Putin. Ukraine is not expected to be on the formal agenda, as Xi is understood to be reluctant to be drawn into what he views as a European matter.

The meeting comes as Trump has strained ties with traditional US allies, at times floating troop withdrawals from South Korea and cuts to assistance for Japan, while his administration continues to describe China as Washington’s main geopolitical rival.

Vuk Vuksanovic, a lecturer in foreign policy and grand strategy at the Department of War Studies, King’s College, London, cautioned against viewing the summit as a new “carve-up” of the world order, however.

“It is a far cry from being a new Yalta,” he said. “In Yalta, you actually had the idea about how the world was going to look, and where the demarcation line would potentially be between the superpowers. We don’t have anything similar, not even the contours of that, in the making at this moment.”

At the Yalta Conference in February 1945, US President Franklin D Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to shape the post-war order, agreeing on the division of Germany and setting the stage for Soviet influence over Eastern Europe.

Where do China-Russia-US relations stand?

There are competing interests at play here.

US and China

Trump landed in Shenzhen on Wednesday, with Xi greeting him at the airport. This is their third in-person meeting since they paused their bitter trade war late last year. At its height, US trade tariffs on Chinese goods reached 145 percent, with China retaliating with tariffs of 125 percent on US goods, before a temporary truce agreed in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025, when tariffs were relaxed. Xi also agreed to pause new restrictions on exports of some rare earth metals which are crucial for manufacturing technology from smartphones to fighter jets. Soon after that, Trump relaxed restrictions on the sale of some Nvidia AI-related computer chips to China.

The truce has since been extended to January 10, 2027 to allow for broader trade talks.

Friction remains, however.

China’s rare earth mineral exports to the US are still about 75 percent below normal levels, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

A scandal over Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company accused of diverting Nvidia chips to China in breach of US export controls, has also strained ties, as has the recent scandal over Nvidia’s former CEO, Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs, including with a woman the US has accused of spying for China.

Beijing rejects all spying allegations as “baseless”, and Trump has said he does not plan to raise the issue at this meeting.

Expectations are low for a major thawing, however: Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, told Al Jazeera that a handshake without incident would be seen as a win.

US and Russia

Trump’s special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, have brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11, the first in direct format since February. The pair have visited both Kyiv and Moscow to promote these talks in recent days.

Days before they travelled to Moscow on Thursday last week, Trump said Washington and Moscow were close to a “big, beautiful agreement” covering not just Ukraine but “all of Europe”.

Trump’s rhetoric towards Putin has softened greatly in recent months, as it has hardened against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom he has publicly admonished for targeting Russian energy facilities, driving up the global cost of oil and diesel. Trump has also called for Zelenskyy to step down and has paused some sanctions on Russian oil, much to the anger of many in his Republican Party.

Some analysts are concerned that US negotiators may offer Russia concessions on NATO in return for peace, including pushing a deal that allows Russia to retain land it has seized from Ukraine in the past four years – a prospect that alarms European leaders.

Russia and China

China has become Russia’s top trading partner since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, weeks after the two had declared a “no limits” partnership.

At a summit in Beijing in May this year, Xi and Putin signed more than 40 cooperation agreements and hailed growing energy trade.

Russian oil exports to China rose 35 percent in the first quarter of 2026, according to a Kremlin aide. China has also ignored Western demands to stop supplying high-tech components to Russia’s weapons industry.

Chinese President Xi Jinping called for China and Russia to “lead and advance the trend towards a multipolar world” after holding talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

The two leaders also met on Wednesday in Shenzhen.

Putin addressed the summit after Xi. He described Western powers as “former hegemons” and said Europe was experiencing a “humiliating decline”.

What does Trump want?

Analysts say Trump is the leader most eager to walk away with something he can present as a “win” from this trilateral meeting.

Vuksanovic said Trump is arriving “wounded domestically” following his Republican Party’s crushing defeat at the US midterm elections, which have seen the Democratic Party gain control of both US Houses of Congress. Trump’s legacy, Vuksanovic added, has been damaged by the war on Iran, particularly in light of Trump’s pledge not to drag the US into another “forever war” during his presidential campaign in 2024.

The deadlock that currently exists between the US and Iran has been described as a “frozen war” by observers.

“[Trump] hopes that he can get some quick-fix deal on something, at least, which he can then try to spin and sell to his base in the US as an enormous accomplishment,” Vuksanovic said. But he added that he doubts Trump could secure anything beyond “something very symbolic”, noting that the agenda of the meeting has remained opaque.

One issue Trump may push for is a trilateral agreement on nuclear armament. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) between Russia and the US lapsed in February. It was first signed in 2010 and caps US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.

Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty after it expired, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing. However, Xi is understood to be unenthusiastic about joining a treaty that China had no part in writing.

Lucas said Trump is there largely “for the photo opportunity”. But he drew a distinction between Trump and his administration, which he said wants to “regain their footing a little bit in terms of leadership” on China.

Washington’s China policy, Lucas said, has been “a disaster”. The administration launched a tariff war that saw duties climb as high as 145 percent, before Beijing retaliated by squeezing exports of rare earth minerals, forcing a truce.

“They’ve got to try to say: ‘Look, we’re leaders. Look, we have a firm policy on China, but one that’s not confrontational,'” he said.

That balancing act is complicated at home, Lucas added, with Republicans in Congress pushing for a tougher line on Beijing as the administration’s position weakens.

What does Putin want?

For Putin, the meeting is above all about the war in Ukraine and ending Russian isolation as a result of European and US sanctions.

“Putin and the Kremlin want cover for the invasion of Ukraine, because they’ve got some serious problems with it,” Lucas said. Moscow wants to keep the Trump camp on side, gain more Ukrainian territory and see Washington withdraw support for Kyiv, he added, while securing at least political backing from Beijing.

Lucas said Russia also wants to break “the notion that it’s isolated” after years of sanctions and the costs of a nearly five-year war that has not delivered victory. Putin is eager to prevent the US sanctions bill, which Trump has paused – and which would impose steep tariffs on Russia and on buyers of its goods, including China – from being implemented.

Vuksanovic said the optics alone, therefore, will be a prize for Moscow. After decades of complaining about US dominance, he said, Russia and China can now argue that “the power gap is not as great, so now we can sit at the table with the US”. That image of great-power status, he added, is “particularly appealing” to Putin.

Lucas added that Putin is unlikely to give up his leverage relating to Iran, and will resist offering Washington any binding promise that Moscow will not cooperate with Tehran.

What does Xi want?

For Xi, the host, the meeting is a chance to secure the space to pursue China’s long-term interests without interference.

“China wants the space to pursue its political, economic and military goals,” Lucas said. Beijing, he added, already has what it wanted in terms of recognition: “Now he’s on the same level with Trump and with Putin.”

What Beijing wants next, Lucas said, is no return to the tariff wars, no opposition to its alternative economic model, recognition of its primacy in rare earth minerals and technology, and no US pushback over Taiwan, which it regards as part of its territory.

China does not want anyone challenging its regional military presence, he said, including the Quad grouping of the US, Japan, India and Australia.

Vuksanovic described China as a rising superpower that is nevertheless “much more inward-looking” and focused on a vast process of internal reform. “They actually much rather prefer to be patient and to think long term, rather than to go for anything which is diplomatically grandiose,” he said.

He argued that China is “probably the biggest winner” of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, which have kept Washington distracted from the Asia Pacific. Beijing’s main worry, he said, is the risk of energy markets collapsing.

“Minus that economic risk, they’re still happy that the US is bogged down in two major wars which Washington does not know how to disentangle itself from,” he said.

Will this meeting change anything on Iran or Ukraine?

Observers are not expecting any sort of a breakthrough from this meeting.

On Iran, Lucas said the US administration would like Beijing to “privately urge the Iranians to make compromises”. But US-Iran talks remain stuck on whether to address the Strait of Hormuz and financial incentives for Tehran first, or its nuclear programme.

Vuksanovic said he is “very dubious” that China would take on a major mediating role. Beyond brokering the Saudi-Iranian rapprochement in 2023, he said, Beijing has preferred to be “diplomatically skilful rhetorically, without sticking out as a major conflict mediator”.

On Ukraine, Vuksanovic said Moscow sees the war as existential and believes it can win through attrition. Russia, he said, will not give up its minimum demands of full control of the Donbas and Ukraine renouncing its bid for NATO membership.

“I don’t think that this meeting will have any bearing on the outcome of the Ukraine war, which will not be resolved at a diplomatic table, but on the battlefield,” he said.

Lucas said Russia will instead try to keep Washington focused on what the Kremlin calls a Europe-wide security architecture, a framing that sidesteps a ceasefire, the territorial question and security guarantees for Kyiv.

Where Moscow and Beijing do agree, Lucas said, is in wanting the US to confine its ambitions of dominance to the Western Hemisphere. But he warned against seeing the summit as a carve-up among equals. “It’s much more a dynamic process where power is shifting, and where these leaders and their administrations are trying to preserve or even regain power,” he said.

What is the rest of the world hoping for?

Above all, stability, Lucas said.

Governments do not want Trump, weakened by the midterms, returning to a tariff war with China or disrupting their own economic ties with Beijing. The European Union faces a looming decision on its own economic relationship with China, he noted, while Canada, under Prime Minister Mark Carney, and the Gulf states are already recalibrating their approach.

“They would like a little bit of space themselves where they’re not having to respond to self-inflicted crises,” Lucas said. “So they’ll want Trump to behave.” They will also hope Putin is open to some pullback in Ukraine, and that China uses its power responsibly.

Vuksanovic said countries of the Global South will welcome the three powers talking, which fits their thinking on multipolarity. But they will also bring “a healthy degree of scepticism”.

“They will primarily observe whether there is any tangible outcome which impacts their own respective interests,” he said, from conflict resolution to the global economy, energy and new technologies.

news.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia Exit Could Hand China's AI Chip Market to Huawei, Analyst Warns as Ban Talk Grows
news.text: Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO could speed up China's shift away from American artificial intelligence chips and hand a larger share of the market to Huawei, a policy adviser said Thursday.George Chen, a partner at advisory firm The Asia Group, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" that Huang's departure could mark the end of a more accommodating U.S. approach to chip sales to China. He said it could also push Beijing harder toward self-reliance in semiconductors.Chen added that Congress could eventually impose a full ban on U.S. chip sales to China, which could give Huawei a bigger slice of the market.The end of Huang's China strategyHuang was one of the most prominent voices in Washington arguing against strict export controls. He warned for years that cutting off Chinese customers would only speed the rise of domestic competitors, especially Huawei.His resignation on Nov. 12 came after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom U.S. officials reportedly suspect of being a Chinese intelligence asset. She is not related to him. The scandal intensified a long-running debate in Washington over exports of advanced AI chips to China.China's Foreign Ministry has called the spy allegation groundless.Even before Huang resigned, Chen highlighted how closely the executive and his company were tied together."Nvidia and Jensen are deeply intertwined," Chen wrote in a note earlier this month. "Many people will say Nvidia without Jensen won't be the same."Nvidia pulls back from ChinaThe company has already started to change course. Interim CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday that Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China. That ends its participation in an arrangement that had allowed some advanced chip sales to the country.The H200 deal was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. It required the chips to be shipped through the U.S. so the government could collect a 25% tariff.Nvidia has also created a board-level committee to oversee national security and export control compliance.Hawks push for tighter rulesChina hawks in Congress have seized on the scandal to push for tougher export restrictions. Lawmakers backing stricter chip control bills say Huang's departure removes one of the strongest voices against them.Dan Ives of Yorkville & Ives Co. called the scandal "a black eye moment for Jensen" that would bring more scrutiny to chip sales to China, a policy Huang had lobbied for.The debate comes as Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet in Shenzhen this week during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Analysts expect chip export policy to hang over the talks.Huawei stands to gainHuawei has spent years building its own AI chips, known as the Ascend series, after U.S. sanctions cut it off from key American technology. Beijing has pushed Chinese companies to adopt domestic chips, and the government has discouraged purchases of some Nvidia products.A full U.S. ban on chip sales would effectively leave the Chinese market to domestic suppliers. That could boost Huawei's revenue and speed up its technology development, though analysts say Chinese chips still trail Nvidia's best products in performance.What's at stake for NvidiaChina was once one of Nvidia's biggest markets, but its share of the company's revenue has shrunk sharply under successive rounds of U.S. export controls. Nvidia's latest results, which included quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion, show that demand elsewhere remains very strong.Still, investors and policymakers are watching closely. Huang is scheduled to give closed-door testimony before three House committees on Dec. 1. Federal investigators are also examining alleged export control violations involving Megaspeed.How Washington handles chip exports after Huang could reshape the global AI chip industry for years.This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial advice.

news.title: Trump Meets Xi and Putin with Nuclear Arms and Two Wars on Table
news.text: SHENZHEN, China: When President Donald Trump meets Thursday with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, it could mark a pivot in world history — or become a quickly forgotten photo op. Trump, who will test his reputation as an expert dealmaker in the trilateral meeting, has promoted his time with Xi and Putin — two of America's leading rivals — as a chance to hash out rules for controlling nuclear arms and to start resolving the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Experts have kept expectations low for major breakthroughs. The president said the advantage of meeting the two autocrats at the same time would be because their countries work together. “They both like Trump. Now, what happens after me? That I can’t tell you,” Trump said in a Thursday interview with Fox News. Trump plans to have a separate one-on-one meeting with Xi — his third substantial meeting with him this year — right before the trilateral. He also added a separate sit-down with Putin to his schedule, marking the first time the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia’s war in Ukraine . Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin , even as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions , while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war. Along for the trip — but so far keeping a low profile — is Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX has intermittently throttled the military-grade Starshield satellite system used by Ukraine for launching its drones and intercepting hits from Russia. One meeting is unlikely to produce a breakthrough in nuclear talks The trilateral is scheduled to occur after a session with leaders at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit on Thursday morning and is expected to be the capstone to Trump's Asia trip that started Tuesday in the Philippines. Trump has said he wants to talk to the leaders about their nuclear stockpiles. The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China . But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles. Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said Trump's showmanship could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals. “We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump at APEC," Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.” Trump told Fox News in his interview that “it’s a very hard thing to do” to ask a leader to reduce nuclear stockpiles. Trump boasts about his relationships. But the ties between Xi and Putin are stronger Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters that Putin, Trump and Xi would likely touch on the war in Ukraine, though the agenda was not fully set. Trump has said he wants to discuss that war — as well as the conflict in Iran. His ambitions recall an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump is negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine — or countries like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks. The U.S. president has openly pursued a Nobel Peace Prize even as he took military action against Venezuela and Iran. He also threatened earlier this year to take Greenland by force from Denmark, a gambit that led to an agreement for the construction of U.S. military bases. Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi appealed to his ego Wednesday by greeting Air Force One on the airport tarmac, as the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug. But Trump does not appear to always have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share. For all the compliments the U.S. president has showered on the two autocrats, the warmth has not always been mutually effusive. news.title: Crude oil futures edge lower as US inventories rise
news.text: Mangaluru Brent crude oil futures traded marginally lower on Thursday morning as official data showed an increase in crude oil inventories for the week ending November 13. https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/topic/CRUDE_OIL/ At 9.31 am on Thursday, January Brent oil futures were at $91.88, down by 0.08 per cent, and January crude oil futures on WTI (West Texas Intermediate) were at $82, down by 0.38 per cent. November crude oil futures were trading at ₹7757 on Multi Commodity Exchange (MCX) during the initial hour of trading on Thursday against the previous close of ₹7694, up by 0.82 per cent, and December futures were trading at ₹7704 against the previous close of ₹7647, up by 0.75 per cent. https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/topic/mcx/ According to the US EIA (Energy Information Administration), commercial crude oil inventories in the US increased 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million barrels, 3 per cent below the five-year average. The four-week average for jet fuel product supplied increased 0.3 per cent year over year.
