news.title: Oil prices settle lower as traders weigh surplus supply outlook
news.text:
Oil prices fell more than 1% on Wednesday after US crude and fuel inventories rose more than expected, according to the Energy Information Administration, adding to expectations of a supply surplus.

Brent crude futures fell $1.19, or 1.28%, to $91.95 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate futures settled down $2.75, ‌or 3.2%, at $83.26, their lowest since August 26. 

Brent fell more than $2 a barrel during the session, while WTI lost more than $4.

US crude inventories rose 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million barrels in the week ended November 13, the EIA said, compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll of a 58,000-barrel rise.

US gasoline stocks rose 5.2 million barrels in the week to 215.9 million barrels, the EIA said, versus analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for a build of 1.6 million barrels.

Distillate stockpiles, which include diesel and heating oil, rose by 1.6 million barrels in the week to 104.9 million barrels, versus expectations for a 1.3 million-barrel rise, the EIA data showed.

Those stock increases renewed selling pressure, Gelber & Associates analysts said, adding: "Attacks involving Iran and commercial shipping ​still threaten deliveries through the Strait of Hormuz, but those risks have provided limited support against the growing expectation of a global surplus."

Meanwhile, both Brent and US crude ​futures contracts were on track for declines of about 20% this month on rising exports from the Middle East, as signaled by plummeting shipping rates.

The Brent/WTI spread was trading at its widest in around two weeks on Tuesday, LSEG data showed, with WTI logging steeper declines during trading on Wednesday.

"WTI arbitrage trades have been shut to Asia and Northwest Europe, thus WTI correcting more ​than Brent is the expected price movement to allow the arbitrage window to open again," said June Goh at Sparta Commodities, adding that rising US Gulf Coast ​crude stocks are further contributing to the widening spread.

US-IRAN CONFLICT CONTINUES

But the continuing Iran war and the risks to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz curbed price declines.

Iran said it attacked US ‌drone and ⁠missile sites in Kuwait overnight after the US struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. It was Iran's first attack on the US-allied Gulf state since September. Bahrain, home of the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, said it intercepted Iranian attacks.

Both oil benchmarks had settled higher on Tuesday as attacks on ships in the Middle East intensified, even as talks continued between Iran and mediators from Oman and Qatar.

ADNOC L&S of the United Arab Emirates said on Wednesday that one crew member was missing and 11 ​injured after one of its vessels was ​attacked in the Strait of Hormuz ⁠on Tuesday.

An LPG tanker was also struck by a projectile off the coast of Oman on Monday, prompting its crew to evacuate the ship.

"Although regional supply may continue to recover through alternative routes, the latest vessel data suggests that normalization of flows ​through Hormuz is still not possible under current conditions," LSEG analysts said on Tuesday.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday ​that they launched five drones ⁠toward two pumping stations along Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which has been used to bypass the strait.

Saudi Arabia is preparing for the conflict with the Houthis to stretch well into next year, said two Western officials briefed on the plans by Saudi officials.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump is expected to hold bilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in China ⁠on Thursday, ​in addition to the trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, US and Russian officials said.

Trump's ​envoys have intensified diplomatic efforts to end Russia's war in Ukraine, with discussions that are also set to involve European leaders focused on post-war security guarantees and economic recovery planning.
news.summary: Oil prices fell more than 1% on Wednesday after US crude and fuel inventories rose more than expected, according to the Energy Information Administration, adding to expectations of a supply surplus.
news.author: Abubakar Ibrahim

news.title: Elon Musk claims no-one has 'helped Ukraine more than I have' after Starlink chaos
news.text: The world's wealthiest man has claimed that no-one has helped Ukraine more than he has. Elon Musk's comment come just weeks after his company throttled the internet service central to the country's defence systems. Speaking to CNBC's Andrew Ross Sorkin on Wednesday, Musk said he has been supportive of Ukraine from before the war began more than four-and-a-half years ago. He also claimed that the entire Ukrainian front would collapse immediately if Starlink were to be disabled . The owner of Starlink said: "It would probably be accurate to say that there is no private individual who has helped Ukraine more than I have. I made sure that Starlink was in Ukraine, prepositioned, ahead of the Russian invasion. When Russia invaded, they disabled all communications, all cell towers, all fibre cable and every satellite communication systems. There was one system they could not disable and that was Starlink." To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed. Musk has said that had Ukraine not had access to Starlink, Russia would have won. "And if they had not had Starlink, their entire line would have collapsed because they would have had no communication system and Russia would have won," the owner of Tesla said. "Now does that sound like a pro-Russian action to you?" The Mirror reported last month that Musk ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink relied on by Ukraine, according to US officials. The decision caused panic in Kyiv and left Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said at the time that he had been "betrayed" by US President Donald Trump after a key part of his country's defences against Russia went down. He claimed that Trump and Musk deliberately blocked Ukraine's access to Starlink overnight after the Ukrainian military faced slowdowns in speed. The satellite internet service is operated by SpaceX, Musk's aerospace company, and provides high-speed broadband globally and is used by Ukraine for military communications and drone operations. Speaking on CNBC, Musk said that Starlink provides the backbone of communications for the Ukrainian military and for Ukraine more broadly. "If we were to turn off Starlink, the entire Ukrainian front would collapse immediately," he said. "This is an action that could only be described as incredibly supportive of Ukraine." Musk also clarified that Starlink is a "civillian system, it is not mean to be used for offensive drone strikes that kill people". He added: "If you want to do that, you need to do Starshield, which is controlled by the US government." "Do not ask me as a private individual to make kill decisions that sometimes result in the loss of innocent lives, not just soldiers. That is not my position to do. And yet we have been pressed relentlessly to do that."
news.summary: "If we were to turn off Starlink, the entire Ukrainian front would collapse immediately," Elon Musk said. "This is an action that could only be described as incredibly supportive of Ukraine."
news.author: Tannur Anders
